title: Why Bullet Train Noses Are So Long (It's Not Wind Drag!) | So That's Why
description:
Japanese Shinkansen bullet trains have pointed noses stretching 15 meters long. Many people think this is just to slice through the air and cut wind drag; even stranger, Taiwan High Speed Rail runs faster than its Japanese parent train, yet its nose is actually shorter! What is going on?

In this episode, the Chief and Little Q head onto the high-speed rail platform and into the tunnels: first seeing where most of a long train's air drag actually comes from, why a train plunging into a tunnel acts like a bicycle pump and fires a loud "boom" at the exit (a tunnel micro-pressure wave), and why the problem only surfaced after switching to concrete slab tracks. Next, they see how a long nose stretches a steep pressure cliff into a gentle slope, what kingfishers and owls taught engineers, what curves came out of firing projectiles through pipes and running supercomputer simulations, and finally the trade-off among speed, tunnel cross-section, and passenger seats—revealing why an 8-meter nose is quiet enough in Taiwan.

The illustrations in this episode were generated with AI; the trains shown are generic illustrations and not specific liveries. The multiples and dimensions mentioned are approximate values from engineering literature and teaching materials; the source for every claim is listed in the references below.

Information as of 2026-11-14

p122.text: No! The secret isn't on the train, it's in Taiwan's tunnels.

p123.text: Recall the pump? In a wider tube, air slips past, making a small wave.
